1.45.m: Bhīṣma said: / Now I desire to hear of the slaying of Hiraṇyakaśipu, / and the glorification of Narasiṃha, which destroys sin.
Pulastya said: / Formerly in the Kṛta age, O king, lord Hiraṇyakaśipu, / the primeval progenitor of the Daityas, performed very great tapas.
For ten thousand years and ten hundred years, / he lived dwelling in the water, maintaining silence and bathing, firm in his vow.
Endowed with tranquility, self-restraint, and celibacy, / Brahmā became pleased with him because of his tapas and discipline.
Then the self-born Lord himself arrived there, / in a celestial chariot radiant like the sun, yoked with swans,
together with the Ādityas, Vasus, Sādhyas, and the deities the Maruts, / with the Rudras, with the Viśvedevas as his attendants, and with Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and serpents;
with the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions, with rivers and oceans, / with the lunar mansions, the muhūrtas, the planets wandering in the sky, and the great grahas;
with the gods and the Brahmarṣis, with the Siddhas and the seven sages, / with the meritorious royal sages, and with hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
The glorious guru of the moving and unmoving, surrounded by all the denizens of heaven, / Brahmā, the foremost of the knowers of Brahman, spoke these words to the Daitya:
"I am pleased with you, my devotee, by this tapas, O one of noble vows. / Choose a boon; may good fortune attend you! Obtain your desired wish as you please."
Hiraṇyakaśipu said: / "May neither gods, Asuras, Gandharvas, nor Yakṣas, serpents, or Rākṣasas, / nor human beings or Piśācas slay me, O best of gods!
May sages and human beings not curse me with curses, O grandfather! / If the Lord is pleased with me, this is the boon chosen by me.
Neither by an edged weapon nor by a missile, neither by a mountain nor by a tree, / neither by something dry nor by something wet, nor by any other means may there be death for me.
May I alone become the sun, the moon, the wind, the fire, / the water, the intermediate space, the lunar mansions, and the ten directions!
May I be wrath, and passion, Varuṇa, Indra, Yama, / the bestower of wealth, the lord of wealth, the Yakṣa, and the lord of the Kiṃpuruṣas!"
Brahmā said: / "This divine, wondrous boon has been granted to you by me, my child. / It bestows all desires, dear one; you will attain it without doubt."
Having spoken thus, the Lord went into the sky, / to the Vairāja abode of Brahmā, frequented by hosts of Brahmarṣis.
Then the gods and Gandharvas, together with the sages and the Cāraṇas, / having heard of this granting of the boon, approached the Grandfather.
The gods said: / "From the granting of this boon, O Lord, the Asura will slay us. / Therefore, O Lord, let a favor be done and let his death also be devised.
The Lord is the primeval creator of all beings, sovereign by himself, / the creator of offerings to gods and ancestors, the unmanifest nature, the Supreme."
Having heard those words beneficial to all the worlds, the god, the Prajāpati, / then comforted them with words that were like extremely cool water:
"Inevitably, O thirty gods, the fruit of tapas must be obtained by him. / At the end of his tapas, the Lord Viṣṇu will carry out his slaying."
Hearing those words from the lotus-born one's mouth, / all the deities departed to their own divine abodes, filled with joy.
As soon as the boon was obtained, the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, / conceited from the grant of the boon, then began to torment all subjects.
In the hermitages, the Dānava assaulted the exalted sages / who had declared their vows, were devoted to truth and dharma, and possessed self-control.
Having conquered the gods dwelling in the three worlds, / the great Asura brought the three worlds under his sway and dwelt in heaven.
When, intoxicated by arrogance from the boon and driven by the law of time, / he made the Daityas entitled to sacrifice and the gods unentitled to sacrifice,
then the Daityas and Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas and Vasus, / the Rudras, the divine hosts, Yakṣas, divine twice-born, and great sages
approached Viṣṇu of great strength, the protector, as their refuge, / the god of gods, embodiment of sacrifice, eternal Vāsudeva.
The gods said: / "O Nārāyaṇa, highly fortunate one, the gods have sought refuge in you! / Protect us, O Lord, and slay the lord of Daityas, Hiraṇyakaśipu!
For you are our supreme benefactor, you are our supreme teacher, / you are our supreme deity, the foremost god of Brahmā and the rest!"
Viṣṇu said: / "Abandon your fear, O immortals! I grant you fearlessness. / Likewise, O gods, re-enter the third heaven without delay.
For this Daitya, together with his host, arrogant from the grant of the boon / and unslayable by the lords of the immortals—I will slay that lord of Dānavas."
Having spoken thus, the imperishable Lord Viṣṇu, protector of the universe, / Hari, the supreme lord, went to the place of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Taking the appearance of the sun in splendor and resembling a second moon in radiance, / he made half of his body that of a man and half of his body that of a lion.
With his man-lion form, holding hand in hand, / he then saw the vast, divine, delightful, mind-pleasing
and radiant assembly hall of Hiraṇyakaśipu, furnished with all desires, / a hundred yojanas wide and one hundred and fifty yojanas long,
hovering in the air, moving at will, five yojanas in height, / free from old age, grief, and fatigue, unshakable, auspicious, and pleasant,
possessing rooms and seats, charming, blazing as if with brilliance, / provided with water within, fashioned by Viśvakarman,
filled with divine-colored trees that yielded fruits and flowers, / blue, yellow, dark black, dusky, white, and red,
and pure bushes bearing red flower clusters; / he saw it floating, resembling a thick white cloud.
Naturally luminous, captivating with divine fragrance, / it was exceedingly pleasant, free from suffering, neither cold nor hot.
Those who reached it experienced neither hunger, thirst, nor weariness; / it was adorned with manifold forms, varied and brilliantly shining.
Surpassing the moon, surpassing the sun, surpassing the radiance of fire, self-luminous, / situated on the vault of heaven, it blazed, illuminating, intensely bright.
All human beings shone in it, filled with joy, / and there was delicious, abundant, and excellent food to eat and consume.
There were garlands of sacred fragrance, trees yielding fruit at all times, / waters cool in heat and warm in cold.
The Lord beheld wish-fulfilling trees whose tips were in blossom, having large branches, / bearing shoots and sprouts, covered with canopies of creeping vines.
There were fragrant flowers, flavorful fruits, / and here and there lakes that were cool and warm.
The Lord saw many sacred waters in his assembly hall, / with blue lotuses, white water lilies, and fragrant hundred-petaled lotuses,
with red water lilies, white water lilies, and blue lotuses, / and with other exceedingly delightful flowers filled with various wonders.
[The lord saw pools] radiant like pure crystal, / with kāraṇḍava ducks, cakravāka birds, cranes, kuraras, and birds with white wings;
resounding with the songs of many swans and the calls of cranes, / and there, fragrant creepers bearing flower clusters.
Glad at heart, the blessed one saw khadira, reed, arjuna, / mango, neem, nāgavṛkṣa, kadamba, vakula, and dhava trees,
priyaṅgus, pāṭalas, silk-cotton trees along with haridravas, / sāl, palmyra, tamāla, and charming campaka trees;
likewise, other flowering trees shone in the hall: / cardamom, kakubha, kaṅkola, lavalī, karṇapūraka,
madhuka, kovidāra, towering as high as many palmyras, / añjana, aśoka, parṇāsa, and many citraka trees,
varuṇa, palāśa, and jackfruit trees together with sandalwood, / blue flowering plants, kadambas, sacred figs, and tindukas,
pārijāta trees, jasmine, deodar pines, / aṭarūṣa, pīlu, and elavāluka trees,
mandāra, kuravaka, punnāga, and kuṭaja trees, / red kuravakas and blue ones, along with agallochum,
kiṃśuka, bhavya, pomegranate, and citron trees, / kāleyaka, dukūla, asafoetida, and tailavartikā plants,
date palms, coconut palms, myrobalans, and madhūkas, / saptaparṇas, bilvas, yāvās, and śarāvatas,
asana and tamāla trees surrounded by various thickets, / and creepers of diverse forms bearing flowers, leaves, and fruits.
These and many other trees born of the forest, / endowed with various flowers and fruits, shone on all sides.
Cakoras, peacocks, intoxicated cuckoos, and mynas / flew about those flowering great trees with blossom-laden boughs.
Perched on the treetops, the red, yellow, and scarlet birds, / the joyful jīvañjīvakas, looked upon one another.
In that hall sat Hiraṇyakaśipu, the lord of Daityas, / seated upon a wondrous throne, ten albas in measure.
Upon that divine throne, radiant like the sun, spread with celestial coverlets, / sat the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, with shining earrings.
The great Daityas then waited upon Hiraṇyakaśipu, / and the foremost Gandharvas sang songs with celestial rhythms.
Viśvācī, Sahajanyā, and the honored Pramlocā, / the divine Saurabheyī, Samīcī, Puñjikasthalā,
Miśrakeśī, Rambhā, Citrabhā, Śrutivibhramā, / Cārunetrā, Ghṛtācī, Menakā, and Urvaśī—
these and thousands of other [apsarases] skilled in dance and song / waited upon the sovereign king Hiraṇyakaśipu.
The sons of Diti, all of whom had obtained boons, attended upon him: / Bali, Virocana, and Naraka the son of the earth,
Prahlāda and Vipracitti, and the great asura Gaviṣṭha, / the slayer of gods, the causer of grief, Samana, and likewise Sumati,
Ghaṭodara, Mahāpārśva, Krathana, Piṭhara, / Viśvarūpa, Svarūpa, and the mighty Viśvakāya,
Daśagrīva, Vālin, the great Asura Meghavāsas, / Ghaṭābha, Viṭarūpa, Jvalana, and Indratāpana.
Those hosts of Daityas and Dānavas all wore blazing earrings; / they were garlanded, armored, and had all observed their vows;
they had all won boons, were valiant, and had their deaths preordained. / These and many others attended upon the sovereign Hiraṇyakaśipu;
all adorned in divine garments, they attended that great-souled one / in celestial cars of various shapes that shone like fires.
Having the splendor of great Indra, their arms adorned with wondrous armlets, / their limbs decorated, the sons of Diti attended upon him from every side.
Such sovereignty as belonged to that lion of Daityas, that great-souled one, / had never been heard of or seen by anyone in the three worlds.
Upon an altar adorned with silver and gold, across an aisle arranged with wondrous gems, / in a hall graced with charming latticed windows, the lord of beasts looked upon [him].
His limbs adorned with golden bracelets and necklaces, blazing with the radiance of the sun's rays, / attended by hundreds of thousands of Diti's sons, the son of Diti was seen by the lord of beasts.
Then, beholding that exalted one who had arrived like the wheel of Time, / his form of man-lion concealed like fire covered by ashes,
The valorous son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, named Prahlāda, / saw the god arrived in a celestial form as a lion.
Seeing him who had assumed an unprecedented form, radiant like a mountain of gold, / all the Dānavas and Hiraṇyakaśipu were astonished.
Prahlāda said: 'O great king, O mighty-armed source of the daityas, / this man-lion form has never been heard of nor seen by me.'
What is this unmanifest, supreme, divine form that has appeared? / My mind foretells, as it were, a terrible destroyer of Daityas!
Dwelling in his body are the gods, oceans, and rivers, / the Himālaya, the Pāriyātra, and whatever other mountain ranges exist;
the moon together with the constellations, the sun together with its rays, / Kubera, Varuṇa, Yama, and Śakra the husband of Śacī;
the Maruts, divine Gandharvas, and sages rich in penance, / the Nāgas, Yakṣas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas of dread prowess;
Brahmā, the gods, and Paśupati indeed wander, positioned upon his forehead, / as well as all immobile and mobile beings;
and you, together with us, surrounded by all the hosts of Daityas, / and your entire assembly hall filled with hundreds of celestial cars;
the entire triad of worlds, O king, and eternal cosmic order— / all this entire universe is seen within this man-lion!
Here are Prajāpati, the great-souled Manu, the planets and lunar conjunctions, the earth and sky, / portents and Time, steadfastness and intellect, delight, truth, penance, and self-restraint;
And the exalted Sanatkumāra, and the Viśvedevas, and all the ṛṣis, / and anger, and desire, and likewise joy, pride, and delusion, and all the ancestors,
Having heard the words of Prahlāda, the lord Hiraṇyakaśipu, / the chief of troops, spoke to all the dānavas and his troops:
“Let this lord of beasts who has assumed an unprecedented form be seized, / or if there is any doubt, let this forest-dweller be slain!”
All those hosts of Dānavas, surrounding the lord of beasts of terrible prowess, / joyfully attempted to terrify him with their might.
Then, uttering a lion's roar, the exceedingly powerful Man-Lion / smashed that entire assembly, his mouth gaping like Death himself.
As the hall was being shattered, Hiraṇyakaśipu himself, / his eyes perturbed with fury, hurled missiles at the lion:
the Rod missile, the most dreadful of all missiles; / the terrible wheel of Time, and likewise the other, Viṣṇu's discus;
the very fierce missile of Brahmā, created for the three worlds, / the wondrous thunderbolt, and the two thunderbolts, the dry and the wet;
the Raudra missile, the fierce trident, the skeleton missile, the club, / the Brahmaśiras missile, and the Brāhma missile as well;
the Nārāyaṇa missile, the missile of Indra, the fire missile, the winter missile, / the wind missile, the churning missile, the skull missile, and the servant missile.
Likewise the irresistible spear, the Krauñca missile, / the stupor-causing and drying missiles, the burning and liquefying ones,
the shaking, cutting, the great weapon of obstruction, / the club of Time, unshakeable, scorching, and possessing great strength,
the whirling and bewitching, the excellent illusion-bearing missile, / the beloved Gāndharva weapon, and Nandaka, the jewel among swords,
the sleep-inducing, crushing, the supreme Vāruṇa weapon, / and the Pāśupata missile, whose course is unhindered—
these divine missiles Hiraṇyakaśipu then unleashed / against Narasiṃha, like oblations into a blazing fire.
With blazing missiles that foremost of Asuras covered the lion, / just as the sun with its rays covers the Himavat in the hot season.
Stirred up by the wind of wrath, that ocean that was the army of the Daityas / instantly flooded everything, as an ocean submerges Maināka.
With barbed darts, nooses, swords, maces, and clubs, / with thunderbolts, lightning bolts, and great many-branched trees,
with mallets, deceptive nooses, stone mortars, boulders, / blazing śataghnīs, and most dreadful rods,
those Dānavas stood with nooses in hand, matching Mahendra's thunderbolt in fury, / their arms and bodies raised up on every side, like young serpents rearing with their hoods.
Their limbs adorned with clusters of golden garlands, their gaping mouths bristling with sharp fangs, / radiant, their bodies horned, they shone like swans amidst Chinese silk.
That Dānava produced an illusion of fire and wind driven together; / but Indra, thousand-eyed and of great splendor, together with the rain-clouds,
quenched that fire with a mighty downpour of water. / When that illusion had been thwarted in battle, however, the Dānava
unleashed an intense, terrible darkness on every side. / As the world was enveloped in darkness and the Daityas seized their weapons,
enveloped in his own splendor like the risen sun, / the Dānavas saw his three-peaked frown in battle,
standing on his forehead like the triple-flowing Gaṅgā on Mount Trikūṭa. / Then, when all illusions were destroyed, the sons of Diti,
the dejected Daityas, fled to Hiraṇyakaśipu for shelter. / Then, blazing with anger as if burning [all] with his brilliance,
when that lord of Daityas was enraged, the world became enveloped in darkness. / The winds—Āvaha, Pravaha, and Vivaha,
Parāvaha, Saṃvaha, the mighty Udvaha, / and the illustrious Parivaha—heralded the terror of portents.
Thus the seven Maruts roaming the sky were agitated; / they are the planets that indeed appear at the destruction of the whole world.
all moved about at will in the sky, agitated; / and the night-wanderer [Moon] moved out of its proper conjunction in the night.
Together with the planets and lunar mansions, the lord of stars [Moon], O tamer of foes, / and the blessed sun became discolored in the sky.
A dark, headless trunk of immense size was seen in the sky; / and the sun, the source of light, cast off black smokiness.
Standing in the sky, the blessed [sun] was repeatedly haloed; / seven dreadful [suns] resembling smoke arose around the sun in the sky.
Planets stood upon the horns of the moon located in the sky; / and Śukra and Bṛhaspati stood on the left and right.
Śani and Mars, possessing the red luster of Mars, / and indeed all sky-wanderers mounted equally together
the peaks slowly, those dreadful planets that revolve at the end of the cosmic age. / And the moon, the dispeller of darkness, together with its asterisms and planets,
did not gladden Rohiṇī, portending the destruction of all moving and stationary beings. / Seized by Rāhu, the moon was struck by meteors.
Blazing meteors moved at will toward the moon. / The god, the ruler of gods, rained blood.
A meteor having the form of lightning fell from the sky with a great roar. / And out of season, all trees blossomed and bore fruit,
and all creepers bore fruit, which [portents] were said to cause the destruction of the Daityas. / Fruits were born within fruits, and likewise flowers within flowers.
They opened and closed their eyes, laughed and wept loudly, / cried out deeply, smoked and blazed:
the idols of all gods, proclaiming a great dread. / Wild beasts and birds, mingling together with domesticated ones,
cried out dreadfully there, as the battle of beasts approached. / Rivers flowed backwards, their waters turbid.
The directions did not shine, filled with red dust. / Sacred trees were in no way worshipped by those worthy of worshipping them.
They were struck down by the speed of the wind, broken and bent low; / and the shadows of all living beings did not shift.
When the sun went to the west at the destruction of the worlds' cosmic age, / then, atop the mansion of the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu,
in the storeroom and armoury, honey settled / for the destruction of the Asuras and for the victory of the gods.
Diverse dreadful portents of grim aspect were seen; / these and many other dreadful forms arose,
indicating battle, for the destruction of the lord of the Daityas. / As the earth trembled on account of that great-souled lord of the Daityas,
hosts of mountain-serpents of immeasurable power fell, / emitting fire from mouths filled with flaming poison.
Serpents with four heads, five heads, and seven heads, / Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkoṭaka, and Dhanañjaya,
Elāmukha, Kāliya, and powerful Mahāpadma; / the thousand-headed, pure-bodied lord whose banner is the golden palm-tree,
Śeṣa Ananta, the great serpent, immovable though he was, trembled. / The subterranean cavities of the earth, dwelling within water,
were shaken all around by the wrath of the lord of the Daityas. / And the dwellers of the nether regions, bearing diverse powers,
though difficult to shake, trembled as Pātāla was suddenly shaken. / Then the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu touched the earth,
his lips bitten in fury, like the primal Boar. / The Gaṅgā, the Bhāgīrathī, the Kauśikī, and the Sarayū,
the Yamunā, the Kāverī, the low-flowing Kṛṣṇaveṇī, / the swift Tuṅgabhadrā, and the river Godāvarī,
the Carmaṇvatī, the Sindhu, and the ocean, the lord of rivers, / the Śoṇa, originating from Melaka, with waters clear as gems,
the Narmadā of auspicious currents, the river Vetravatī, / the Gomatī crowded with cattle herds, the eastern Sarasvatī,
the Mahākāla-mahī, and the Tamasā bearing flowers; / Jambūdvīpa, possessing jewels and adorned with all varieties of gems,
the Suvarṇapuṭaka adorned with golden mines, / the great river Lauhitya, the mountain adorned with gold,
the city of silk-weavers, Kaśa rich in silver mines, / the Magadhas, the great villages, the Puṇḍras, and the fierce tribes,
the Srughnas, Mallas, Videhas, Mālavan people, Kāśis, and Kosalas; / the abode of Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā, was shaken by the lord of the Daityas,
which was built by Viśvakarman in the shape of Mount Kailāsa's peak; / and the terrifying sea named Lauhitya, whose waters are like jewels.
And the great mountain Udaya, a hundred yojanas high, / having golden altars, glorious, frequented by rows of clouds;
shining with gold-like trees resembling the sun, / with blooming sāla, tāla, tamāla, and karṇikāra trees;
and the renowned Ayomukha, adorned on all sides with minerals; / and the auspicious Malaya mountain, scented with forests of tamāla;
The Surāṣṭras and the Bāhlīkas, the Śūdras and likewise the Ābhīras, / the Bhojas, the Pāṇḍyas, and the Vaṅgas, the Kaliṅgas, the Tāmraliptakas.
likewise the Pauṇḍras, the Śubhras, the Vāmacūḍas with the Keralas; / and the gods and hosts of apsarases were shaken by that Daitya;
and the abode of Agastya, which was made by Agastya of old, / scattered with troops of Siddhas and Cāraṇas, enchanting,
having diverse wondrous birds, large trees in bloom, / with peaks made of gold, frequented by hosts of apsarases;
and the mountain Puṣpitaka, magnificent and pleasant to behold, / which rose up cleaving the ocean, the resting place of the moon and the sun,
which shone with its great peaks, as if scraping the sky, / resembling the rays of the moon and the sun, surrounded by ocean waters;
and the glorious Vidyuttvat mountain, stretching a hundred yojanas, / upon which best of mountains flashes of lightning strike down;
and the glorious mountain Ṛṣabha, standing like a bull; / the glorious mountain Kuñjara, the auspicious home of Agastya;
and the invincible city of serpents called Vimalā, Mālatīpurī, / and likewise Bhogavatī was shaken by that lord of Daityas;
and the Mahāsena mountain, and the Pāriyātra mountain, / and the best mountain Cakravat, and the Vārāha mountain;
and the auspicious city Prāgjyotiṣapura, made of gold, / in which dwelt the wicked-minded Dānava named Naraka;
and the best mountain Megha, with a sound deep like a cloud, / where there are sixty thousand mountains, O ruler of men;
and the great mountain Meru, resembling the morning sun, / whose caves are continually frequented by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Gandharvas;
the mountain Hemagarbha, Mahāsena, and Meghasakha; / and Kailāsa, lord of mountains, was shaken by the lord of Dānavas;
by him the Vaikhānasa lake covered with golden lotuses [was shaken], / and Lake Mānasa, teeming with geese and kāraṇḍava ducks, was shaken;
the best mountain Triśṛṅga, and Kumārī, the excellent river, / and the mountain Mandara, covered with heaps of snow;
and the mountain Uśīrabīja, and the king of mountains Bhadraprastha, / and the mountain Prajāpati, and likewise the mountain Puṣkara;
and the mountain Devābha, and likewise the mountain Vaivālukā, / Krauñca, the mountain of the Seven Ṛṣis, and the mountain Dhūmravarṇa.
These and other mountains, lands, and territories, / and all the rivers along with the oceans, were shaken by the Dānava.
And Kapila, son of the earth, and Vyāghravat were shaken, / as well as the sky-farers, the sons of night, and the dwellers of the netherworld;
likewise the other fierce host, Megha by name, weaponed with elephant goads, / soaring upward with terrible speed—all these were shaken.
Armed with mace and trident, dreadful, Hiraṇyakaśipu, / thundering like a dense raincloud, swift as a storm cloud,
that arrogant son of Diti, enemy of the gods, rushed against the Man-Lion. / He was struck then by that king of beasts with sharp, great claws.
en: Then, with the syllable Oṃ as his aid, having torn [him] apart, he was slain in battle. / The earth, the moon, the sky, the planets together with the sun, and all the quarters trembled.
en: And the rivers, mountains, and great oceans regained their serenity through the destruction of Diti's son. / Then the gods and the ascetics whose wealth is austerity were overjoyed.
en: They praised the eternal primal god with divine names: / 'That this body of the Man-Lion was assumed by you, O God,
en: people knowing the higher and lower will indeed worship this very form.' / Brahmā said: 'You are Brahmā, and Rudra, and Mahendra, the best of the gods.
en: You are the creator and the transformer of the worlds, the imperishable source, / the supreme attainment, the highest essence, the supreme secret, and the highest oblation.
en: And the supreme dharma, and the highest renown—they call you the foremost, supreme, ancient one; / the supreme truth, the highest austerity, the supreme purifier, and the highest path;
en: the supreme sacrifice, and the highest offering—they call you the foremost, supreme, ancient one; / the supreme body, and the supreme Brahman, the highest yoga, and the supreme speech;
en: the supreme secret, and the highest goal—they call you the foremost, supreme, ancient one.' / Having spoken thus, the blessed grandfather of all the worlds,
en: having praised the divine Nārāyaṇa, the lord went to the world of Brahmā. / Then, while musical instruments sounded and Apsarases danced,
en: Lord Hari, the ruler, went to the northern shore of the milk ocean. / The god, exceedingly radiant, having set aside the body of the Man-Lion,
en: [and] having assumed his ancient form, he whose emblem is Garuḍa departed / in a chariot with eight wheels, endowed with splendour and radiant.
en: The lord, the god whose nature is unmanifest, went to his own abode.

1.46.m: en: Glorious Bhīṣma said: / 'The glorification of Narasiṃha has been spoken by you in detail; / so let the glorification of Bhava, of Bhairava, be related.'
en: Pulastya said: / 'Hear also the excellent deed of that god of gods. / There was a Daitya named Andhaka, resembling a heap of crushed collyrium,
en: endowed with great austerity, indeed invulnerable to the dwellers of heaven. / Once, having seen the all-pervading Mahādeva sporting with Pārvatī,
en: he then set about to abduct the goddess: / 'If I abduct this goddess today, he will meet his death in separation [from her].
en: Then this woman, beautiful among the worlds, will become my steady wife.' / [He thought of her] bimba-like lips, charming countenance, and exceedingly lovely face:
en: 'If she should not become my wife, what is the purpose of life?' / Having settled on this intention, and having deliberated with his ministers,
en: he assembled his army and spoke to the commander: / 'Bring me my victorious chariot, the overthrower of gods.
en: I shall conquer all the gods headed by Viṣṇu and Rudra; / I shall carry off the daughter of the mountain; my mind has been stolen by her.'
en: And the slaying of Kanaka by the gods was reported to him by a minister— / [the slaying] performed by the gods with Indra [against him] who had grown attached to another's wife.
en: Then, with his mind overwhelmed with wrath, [he thought], 'I shall kill the gods together with Śaṅkara.' / Having killed that Dānava, Śakra, out of fear of Andhāsura,
en: seeking refuge, went to Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara. / Having seen and bowed to the lord of gods, who has the half-moon as his crest,
en: terrified, he who possesses a thousand eyes made a petition: / 'Grant me freedom from fear, O God, from the Dānava Andhaka.
en: I am afraid of him; today his son was struck down by me in battle. / Therefore, as long as that great Asura does not know his son is slain,
en: so long let him who brings fear to me be quickly killed while still remaining there. / The cruel Dānava, through lust for women, is an abductor of others' wives;
en: he must be slain by you by all means, O best of the gods.' / Having heard these words of Śakra, Śaṅkara, the refuge of all, then
en: gave him freedom from fear, saying to the performer of a hundred sacrifices, 'Do not fear.' / Having been granted freedom from fear, [Śiva] then came from Kailāsa to Kuśasthalī,
en: surrounded by hosts of spirits, for the sake of slaying Andhaka. / Having assumed a form with a huge body, universal-formed, exceedingly terrifying,
en: formidable with flaming, darting serpents like terrifying snakes, / [filling] the sky with matted locks like manes, with the blaze of the crest-gems of serpents' hoods,
en: burning intensely with splendours like the fire of Time at the cosmic dissolution, / with mouths marked by sprout-like fangs, radiant like the digit of the crescent moon,
en: having the appearance of the hollow of the nether world, roaring with terrifying roars, / holding many weapons with many thousands of arms,
en: richly adorned with many ornaments, roaring dreadfully in battle, / wearing a lion-skin as a garment, having a tiger-skin as an upper garment,
en: making a display with an elephant-hide, swarming with the sounds of falling bees— / having assumed such a form that brought fear to Danu's sons and Daityas,
en: the terrifying one descended to earth, bringing destruction to the sons of Danu. / The Danu-born Andhāsura as well, having heard that his son was killed in battle,
en: seized by anger and darkness, ordered the battle-drums [sounded]. / Having gathered [his forces] and being vigilant, he arrived where those gods stood,
en: together with a great army equipped with chariots and elephants. / Those gods, seeing the Dānavas eager for a great combat,
en: with their armour cast off, fled and sought refuge with Śambhu. / Saying 'Do not fear' to those gods, the three-eyed god,
en: taking up his trident, stood firm, bearing the sound of gnashing teeth in wrath. / Then by the enraged Andhaka, with a hundred crore arrows, the hosts
en: of many gods, united together, were also struck down. / Releasing sparks of radiance like fire, the wielder of Pināka
en: then completely enveloped Andhaka, who stood in his chariot, with arrows. / Then the lord of Danu's sons, standing in his chariot, slackened, his weapons slipping,
en: summoned all the Dānavas and began to fight. / In many ways that army was broken by warriors fighting with various weapons,
en: slain in battle by the heroic gods who had taken refuge in friendship with Sthāṇu. / And the Dānava Andhaka, seeing his army broken by the gods,
en: and himself obstructed by Maheśa with crores of arrows, / with his body distressed, relying solely on courage,
en: seized the very Pināka of Rudra and struck Rudra. / From the blow of Pināka, Rudra then fell to the ground.
en: When the god fell to the ground, the three worlds shook; / the oceans abandoned their shore, and mountains [lost] their peaks;
en: disjoined stars fell loosened in large numbers. / When the lord of gods had fallen to the earth, Andhaka again with a mace
en: angrily struck the serpent; having struck him, he knocked him to the ground. / Leaving Śiva, the king of serpents fled elsewhere.
en: Regaining consciousness after a moment, the Supreme Lord arose; / taking up his divine axe, he did not see the Dānava at all.
en: Having created an illusion of darkness, being skilled in a hundred illusions, / when the god was bewildered by it, where indeed did the Dānava go?
en: Having incurred fear from Śambhu, what will the wicked one do now? / While the gods were covered by darkness and fell into confusion,
en: their forces having their minds bewildered, they then spoke because of the gravity of the matter. / In the meantime, the sun, remaining in the form of brilliance,
en: arose in human form, making the directions free from darkness. / When the darkness was destroyed and the firefly stood revealed with delighted limbs,
The gods attained joy, with their faces and eyes brightened; / and all the gods blazed up, [along with] the hosts led by Skanda.
They praise the Sun in human form with various hymns, / peerless, all-pervading, beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
having the glossy hue of smooth coral, glowing bright like red vermilion; / seeing him shining then, embracing the earth with the five limbs of the body,
ready to bow down again, preceded by profound meditation, / beholding that god of gods with an affectionate glance, the three-eyed Lord,
Hara slowly spoke to the god with an affectionate and deep voice, / as the Lord seemed to fill the three worlds with his splendors:
"For living beings overcome by Daitya illusion, their minds agitated in perception, / this alone is the one infallible deity.
Indeed, this very god, the sovereign Lord, carrying beings across / the entire ocean of worldly existence, acts as a helmsman.
Worshiping with devotion this god, manifold beings always / become fit for the highest good; I bow to that all-pervading Sun,

who, on the peak of the mountain of dawn, with rays acting as a playful crown, / brilliant like blossoms, pervading the cardinal and intermediate directions / with assemblies of his own beams, blazes forth for prosperity in the world;

who, by Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, the Maruts, Acyuta, Agni, and the lord of waters, / and by assemblies of chief ṛṣis skilled in rites, desiring the highest good every day / with daylight ointments, have all their bodies anointed with divine perfumes;

whose form is ever worthy of worship at the dissolution by the Vedas, / with words adorned with varied garlands of verses; / those who praise you in another's house, bereft of homes, / their hands perpetually outstretched on earth—they become [prosperous].

Men who are afflicted in limbs with ringworm, leprosy, and boils, / with withered skin, bad nails, and lost hair and noses— / O Lord of gods, when they bow to your feet, / they instantly become humans with the form of sixteen-year-olds.

For the singers of the Sāman sing of you as the Sāman for the sake of sacrifice, / the Adhvaryu priests and the hosts of chief Ṛgvedic priests as the Ṛg verse, / those skilled in duties know you as the noble one to be approached, / and the ancestors [know you] as the Nagas and the all-fragrant one.

And the Upaniṣad speaks of you as Māyā, O Sun; only six gods / and mortals worship you here as we do, / along with the hosts of Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Cāraṇas; / and thus, O Lord, you assume various forms.

Those who do not continually revere your light worthy of adoration, / devoid of wealth, with their skies burned by rays, / their throats and bellies emaciated with hunger, with a pot-potsherd / wander for alms in others' houses, destitute of wealth and sons.

With wide eyes like the interior of an open red lotus, / with slightly playfully moving and curved tawny pupils, / enchanting, charming with very praiseworthy necklaces, / wearied under the burden of lofty, swelling breasts,

with thighs like plantain trunks, with broad and plump round hips, / bound with a ringing, jingling girdle of tinkling gems, / a multitude of noble matrons whose faces are adorned with golden veils, / the hem of their garments hanging from the top edge of their foreheads,

speak sweetly and falteringly in their homes, / made resonant with the jingling sound of anklets, / beloved to those whose hands [give gifts] to Agni, radiant like the moon— / by whom, O Lord, you who grant release from worldly existence, are worshiped.

You alone are Brahmā, you are Hari, you are the wind, you are fire; / you are Rudra, you are Death, you are Varuṇa, you are the lord of immortals; / you are Soma, you are Vāyu, you are the earth, and you are Īśvara; / you are sacrifice, you are the lord of wealth, you are the invincible one.

Those seven steeds, unyoked in the sky by heaven's drivers, / roam effortlessly upon the earth, crossing its wide expanse; / having traversed around this sky that has no boundary, / these never succumb to the slightest fatigue."

Devoted solely to the yoga of meditation, meditating through absorption on your fourth state, O you of infinite forms, / embodied beings, freed from affliction and joined to fearlessness, [attain] that eternal, inconceivable, beginningless, and endless Brahman,

Free from birth and diseases, supreme, ancient, the Lord, beyond old age, death, sorrow, and fear, / unmeasured by assemblages of gross perception, pure, which is fully revered by exponents of Vedānta.

Having worshipped you, whose form is a mass of fire, the dwelling of austerities, for a very long time, devotees have gone to heaven, / O Sun, the pure, charming form whose pair of lotus feet is rubbed by the heads of crowds of gods and demons!

O Lord of beings, granter of boons to beings, constantly imperishable Self, O Savitṛ, whose loud laughter fills the sky, sole lamp of the world, / the very dwelling of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus mantras, cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, guardian of the worlds!

For me, wretched and miserable in birth after birth, whose desires of thought have drowned in the ocean of worldly existence, / may the fearful affliction of old age, death, sorrow, and disease, which constantly [assails] the inner self, [be averted], O Lord of ascetics whose rays are like the moon!
Whoever recites this in the morning, evening, or at midday, [a hymn] of the blazing-rayed [Sun], / attains the world of the Sun and obtains dharma, wealth, and desires.
And constantly whatever is cherished in his heart [is obtained] from the Sun. / Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, who brings fearlessness to devotees!
O Subrahmaṇya, salutations to you, who are bowed to by all the gods! / Salutations to you indeed, O sharp-rayed one; salutations to the eye of the world!
Salutations to you, O maker of light; O Sun, be victorious, O Lord of the world! / I am tormented by this chief of Danus, O Lord of the world.
What shall I do, and how may I slay him, O maker of the day? / The Sun said: 'Conquer with the trident the most wicked one, who is skilled in a hundred illusions.
Attain victory, O Lord of the gods, having slain Andhaka with your trident!' / Taking the trident then, casting it from afar with Hara's splendor,
Then the evil-doing Andhaka struck with a trident. / In that battle Rudra, indeed afflicted by Andhaka,
Discharged an exceedingly fierce arrow, namely the Pāśupata; / bending the Pināka bow with his arms, the wielder of the Pināka, Śaṅkara himself [shot it].
From the piercing by Rudra's arrow, from the blood of Andhaka, / Andhakas were born by the hundreds and then by the thousands.
As they were being ripped open, from their blood other / terrible Andhakas arose again, by whom the entire world was pervaded.
Seeing that deceitful Andhaka, the God of gods / then created the Mothers in order to drink the blood of Andhaka:
Māheśvarī, and Brāhmī, Saurī, Bāḍavī, / Sauparṇī, and Vāyavyā, Śaṅkhinī, and Taittirī,
Saurī, Saumyā, Śivadūtī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Vāruṇī, / Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Vibhāvarī,
Śatānandā, Bhagānandā, Picchilā, Bhagamālinī, / Bālā, Atibalā, Raktā, Surabhī, Mukhamanḍitā,
Mātṛnandā, Sunandā, Biḍānī, and Śakunī, / Revatī, of great merit, and likewise Śikhipaṭṭikā.
And then the destroyer of Tripura pierced the Daitya with his trident; / the Mothers then drank the blood that flowed from him.
Drained of blood, O king, the Daitya became dried up; / impaled upon the trident, the Daitya remained then for a thousand divine years.
Though held by the mighty Rudra, he did not die. / Then Śambhu was praised with devotion by that Daitya, O you of noble vows:

'Salutations to Śambhu, the cause of the destruction of worldly existence! Salutations to you, O best of gods, be pleased! / You are earth, water, fire, wind, ether, sun, moon, and the sacrificer—having eight forms, the creator of worldly existence, the all-sufficient!

Bāṇa, having pleased you with many musical instruments, obtained lordship in his own city, which is to be guarded by you; / the lord of Rākṣasas, having weighed the mountain with his arms and appearing tormented by your stepping [upon it], praised you.

He obtained lordship over all the host of Rākṣasas and also an exalted son, the binder of Śakra. / O Hara, remover of the fear of rebirth, supremely generous, bringer of my happiness, essence of all the gods,

You who have conquered the wind, skilled in granting desired wishes! In this battle, your lotus feet are the essential refuge. / That man who places your lotus foot in his heart, O Lord, you grant his desire everywhere, moved by his devotion.

In ancient times, chiefs of sages, having thus worshipped you, Hara, in the form of the Liṅga with reverence, attained their wishes; / contemplating you as the sole source of existence, having the form of the five elements, residing in the hollow of a tree, as the life of all living beings,

One obtains all desires from meditating on your feet, O Lord, having arrived at your place accompanied by your servants at every step. / I am a fool; I do not know how to praise you, O lover of your devotees!
Even with an attitude of an enemy, he who enters battle is pitied by the supreme Lord.' / Having been thus praised with devotion and respect by the Daitya, Maheśa
Granted him the status of a Gaṇa leader, with the name Bhṛṅgirīṭin. / This glory of Hara, the remover of mundane existence, has been related to you, O king;

Named as the destroyer of obstacles, it brings happiness to those devoted to him.
Bhīṣma said:
[Explain] divinity, happiness, kingship, wealth, fame, for a man,
Victory, enjoyment, and health, longevity, knowledge, prosperity, a son, / kinsmen, and all well-being—tell me, O best of Brahmins.

Pulastya said:
Endowed with these qualities, the Brahmin on earth is always glorious; / in the three worlds, the Brahmin-god is always pure in age after age.
Having honoured the twice-born, the gods enjoy imperishable heaven, / kings protect the earth, and the worlds enjoy wealth, happiness, and auspiciousness.
There is no one in the world equal to a Brahmin; he is a deity even to the gods; / he consists of dharma itself visibly on earth and bestows liberation abundantly.
He is the venerable guru of the worlds, a sacred place in human form, free from sin, / an abode of all deities, a being created by Brahmā in ancient times.
This matter was asked of the grandfather [Brahmā] by Nārada in ancient times: / 'When who is worshipped, O Brahmā, does Mādhava become pleased?'

Brahmā said:
'He with whom the Brahmins are pleased, Viṣṇu is pleased with him; / therefore, one eager to serve Brahmins attains the supreme Brahman.
Viṣṇu always dwells in the bodies of Brahmins, not otherwise; / therefore, when a Brahmin is worshipped, Viṣṇu is pleased that very moment.
Whoever constantly worships Brahmins with gifts, honor, adoration, and the like, / by him a hundred sacrifices with abundant sacrificial gifts have been performed in accordance with the injunctions.
The mouth of a Brahmin is a field free of salt soil and free of thorns; / one should sow all seeds [there]—that is an eternal cultivation.
Whatever is given after approaching, and whatever gift is delightful, / an end to the ocean can be found, but no end to that gift can be found.
Those who do not harm an earthly god even in mind, even if he is an aggressor, / attain a state agreeable to the heart, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
In whose house a learned man having arrived does not meet with despair, / his sins are all destroyed, and he enjoys imperishable heaven.
Whatever wealth one offers to a Brahmin in proper time, place, and to a worthy recipient, / know that wealth to be imperishable; it endures in birth after birth.
He does not fall into poverty, nor does he become sick or despondent; / having worshipped the twice-born, he obtains a wife agreeable to his heart.
Even having performed reckless deeds, if he gives to a Brahmin on sacred occasions, / that gift is proclaimed to have good qualities, bringing fearlessness and gain.'

The hand that is bruised by rubbing the soles of a brāhmaṇa's feet
is truly called an auspicious hand; any other hand is merely a manual laborer.

Those purified by the dust of a brāhmaṇa's feet, and purified by the drops of their [wash-]water,
always freed from calamities and sins, go to heaven.

Courtyards of houses that are purified by the dust of a brāhmaṇa's feet and clean,
become equal to sacred sites and are praised in sacrificial rites.

In the beginning, the faultless brāhmaṇa was born anciently from the mouth of Brahmā;
the Vedas were produced right there as the cause of creation and preservation.

Therefore, the Vedas were placed in the mouth of the brāhmaṇa by the Supreme Person
for the worship of all the worlds and indeed for the sake of all sacrifices.

In ancestral sacrifices, in marriages, in fire rituals, in rites of appeasement,
and in all benedictory rites, brāhmaṇas are always commended.

The gods consume the oblations, the demons such as Bali and the spirits,
and the ancestors indeed consume the ancestral offerings only through the mouth of the brāhmaṇa.

Whatever gift, oblation, or offering one gives in sacrificial rites
to the gods and to the ancestors is fruitless without a brāhmaṇa.

The demons, spirits, Daityas, and Rākṣasas consume it there;
therefore, one should summon a brāhmaṇa and have those rites performed by them.

[What is given] at the proper time, place, and to a worthy recipient bears a hundred thousand and ten million times the fruit.
Having seen a twice-born, one should offer a salutation with faith.

By his word, a man becomes long-lived and lives for a long time;
from failing to salute, from hatred of brāhmaṇas, and from lack of faith,

the lifespan of men diminishes, and there is loss of prosperity and a miserable condition.
There is increase of life, increase of fame, and increase of learning and wealth;

by worshiping the twice-born, one becomes the best, there is no doubt about this.
Houses that are not muddied by water from the feet of brāhmaṇas, that are not made resonant by the Vedas and Śāstras,

and that are devoid of the utterances svāhā, svadhā, and svasti, are equal to cremation grounds.
Nārada said:
Which brāhmaṇa is the most worthy of worship, and who is unworthy of worship?

Tell me truly the characteristics of a brāhmaṇa, and also of a guru.
Brahmā said:
A learned Vedic scholar who is endowed with good conduct is always worthy of worship,

of good behavior, free from impurities, a veritable sacred place, a sinless person.
Nārada said:
Father, who is born a learned Vedic scholar—in a good family or in a bad family?

Or is the performer of good or bad deeds, which brāhmaṇa is worshipful on earth?
Brahmā said:
One born in a family of true Vedic scholars, if devoid of righteous action, is not at all worshiped.

One born of an unworthy womb and family is worshipful, just as Vyāsa and Vaibhāṇḍaka [are];
Viśvāmitra, born in the lineage of Kṣatriyas, is equal to me.

Vasiṣṭha was the son of a courtesan, and there are other perfected twice-born and sages;
therefore, hear, my son, the characteristic of true Vedic scholars and others,

who have become sacred places on earth and remove all sins:
By birth one is known as a brāhmaṇa; through rituals of consecration one is called twice-born;

through sacred knowledge one attains brāhmaṇa-hood; by all three one has the characteristics of a learned Vedic scholar.
Purified by knowledge, purified by mantras, and likewise purified by the Veda,

and pure through bathing in sacred waters and the like, a brāhmaṇa is remembered as most worshipful,
always devoted to Nārāyaṇa, and of pure inner faculty,

having subdued the senses, conquered anger, impartial toward all people,
devoted to the guru, gods, and guests, and intent on serving his parents,

whose mind never delights in another's wife,
who constantly narrates the Purāṇas, an unbroken lineage of religious storytelling,

By the mere sight of him, the fruit born of horse sacrifices and the like is attained daily;
in conversation with him, one attains the state [resulting from] bathing in the Bhāgīrathī.

Purified by diverse vows, daily bathing, and worshiping the twice-born,
he should be compassionate to friend and foe, and impartial toward all people;

one who does not seize another's property, even a blade of grass lying in the forest,
a man freed from lust, anger, and the rest, unconquered by the senses,

who does not accept another's wife even in thought, when she has come to his house.
Nārada said:
What is the definition of the Gāyatrī, or the virtue born from each of its syllables?

she is white-complexioned, has fire as her mouth, and the sage is Viśvāmitra;
she has mounted Brahmā's head, her tuft of hair is Viṣṇu, and she resides in the heart.

Her application is in the sacred thread ceremony, and she was born in the lineage of Sāṅkhyāyana;
she is known to have the three worlds as her feet, and she resides in the belly of the earth.

In twenty-four bodily places, beginning with the feet and ending with the head,
by placing the twenty-four syllables, one attains the world of Brahmā.

Having known the deity of each syllable, one attains union with Viṣṇu.
Moreover, I shall declare the definitive characteristics of the Gāyatrī:

Seven, five, and then the eighteen-syllabled Yajus formula of Brahman;
beginning with fire and ending with the sound "ha", standing in water one should chant it a hundred times.

From ten million secondary sins, and even from heinous sins,
and freed from sins like killing a brāhmaṇa, they go to my abode.

[Saying:] "To the speech of fire in the man, pleased by the Yajurveda, drink the Soma, svāhā!"
The mantra of Viṣṇu, the great mantra, and likewise that of the Great Lord [Śiva],

of the Goddess, the Sun, Gaṇeśa, and likewise of the sacrifice-consumers, O son,
in whatever family he is born, if endowed with those virtues,

a brāhmaṇa, directly consisting of Brahman, should be worshiped with effort.
And one should give gifts according to rule, always on every festive occasion;

the giver attains inexhaustible [fruit] for hundreds of millions of births.
A brāhmaṇa devoted to the study of the Veda, who recites and teaches others,

and proclaims dharma in the world, righteous conduct, the Śruti, and the Smṛti,
truly the compilations of the Purāṇas, and likewise the compilations of dharma,

having recited them among the people and having recited them among the twice-born,
he, equal to Viṣṇu on earth, is to be worshiped by men and gods.

His strength is inexhaustible; having performed worship equal to that of
such a faultless person who has become a sacred site, a man goes to the abode of Acyuta.

If by chance a sin is committed, a brāhmaṇa is not stained by sins,
just as the sun and fire remain [unpolluted] in the house of an outcaste.

From officiating at sacrifices, from teaching, from marriage, and likewise from accepting gifts from the unworthy,
there is no fault for brāhmaṇas; the twice-born are equal to fire and the sun.

Engaged in breath-control, they destroy in this world the sins
arising from acceptance of gifts, just as the wind [disperses] a cloud in the sky.

He who recites the Gāyatrī daily accompanied by breath-control,
associated with the deities of each syllable, and applies it to his own limbs,

freed from all sins, even those committed in ten million births,
having attained the status of Brahmā, he goes beyond primordial matter.

Therefore, O Nārada, chant the Gāyatrī combined with breath-control.
Nārada said:
How are the breath-controls performed, O Brahman, and who are the deities of each syllable?

therefore, having contracted the anus, one should unite it with the prāṇa;
then, O son, having performed inhalation and the supreme retention of breath,

and having performed three breath-controls, a twice-born should chant the Gāyatrī.
Whoever chants with this alone, his accumulation of grave sins

and minor sins goes to destruction by just a single recitation.
He who, knowing the tone of each syllable, places them on his body,

that person attains the state of Brahman; we are not able to describe the fruit.
Hear the deity of each syllable, my son; I shall declare it.
Muttering which, a twice-born does not drink a mother's breast again. / The first [syllable] is to be known as belonging to Agni, and the second to Vāyu;
the third has Sūrya as its deity, and the fourth likewise has Vāyu; / the fifth has Yama as its deity, and the sixth is declared to belong to Varuṇa;
the seventh belongs to Bṛhaspati, and they know the eighth to belong to Parjanya; / the ninth is to be known as belonging to Indra, and the tenth likewise to the Gandharvas;
know the eleventh as belonging to Pūṣan, and the twelfth is remembered as belonging to Mitra; / the thirteenth is to be known as belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ, and the fourteenth to the Vasus;
the fifteenth belongs to the Maruts, and the sixteenth is remembered as belonging to Soma; / the seventeenth belongs to Aṅgiras, and after that belongs to the Viśvedevas;
the nineteenth belongs to the Aśvins, and the twentieth belongs to Prajāpati; / the twenty-first syllable is to be known as comprising all the gods;
the twenty-second is to be known as belonging to Rudra, and after that is to be known as belonging to Brahmā; / the twenty-fourth belongs to Viṣṇu. These are the deities of the syllables.
Contemplating them at the time of muttering, one would attain complete union with them. / Having known its deities, all speech becomes known to him.
Freed from all sins, he goes to the state of Brahman. / A wise man should first place the Gāyatrī upon his own body,
in twenty-four places, from the feet up to the head. / The wise yogin should place the syllable "tat" on the big toe;
the syllable "sa" on the region of the ankle, and the syllable "vi" on the shanks; / the syllable "tur" on the middle of the knees, and the syllable "va" on the region of the thighs;
the syllable "re" on the private parts, and the syllable "ṇi" on the testicles; / the syllable "yaṃ" on the region of the hips, and the syllable "bha" on the circle of the navel;

having placed the syllable "go" on the belly, he should place the syllable "de" on the breasts; / having placed the syllable "va" on the heart, [he should place] the syllable "sya" on the region of the hands;
having placed the syllable "dhī" on the mouth, he should place the syllable "ma" on the palate; / [he should place] the syllable "hi" on the tip of the nose, and the syllable "dhi" on the eyes;
the syllable "yo" between the eyebrows, and the syllable "yo" on the forehead; / the syllable "naḥ" on the eastern face, and the syllable "pra" on the southern face;
having placed the syllable "co" on the west, he should place the syllable "da" on the north; / having placed the syllable "yāt" on the crown of the head, he abides all-pervading.
Having placed these, the righteous one, having the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, / a great yogin, possessing great knowledge, reaches supreme nirvāṇa.
Listen again to the placement of syllables at the twilight period as it truly is: / having placed "bhūḥ" on the heart, one should place "bhuvaḥ" on the head;
"svaḥ" on the crest-lock; "tat savitur vareṇyam" on the body; / "bhargo devasya dhīmahi" on the two eyes;

one should place "dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt" on the two hands; / "āpo jyotī raso'mṛtaṃ brahma bhūr bhuvaḥ svar om." / By the mere touch of water with this [formula], purified from sin, he goes to Hari:

—bhūḥ —bhuvaḥ —svaḥ —mahaḥ —janaḥ —tapaḥ —satyam / —'tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt'

—'āpo jyotī raso 'mṛtaṃ brahma bhūr bhuvaḥ svar om' / Having thus recited thrice at twilight with breath retention [the mantra] accompanied by the vyāhṛtis, with the praṇava, and containing twelve Oṃkāras,
and muttering the twenty-four-syllabled Sāvitrī during the worship of the sun, / he becomes superior in great knowledge [and] attains the state of Brahman.
Listen attentively, my son, to the Gāyatrī characterized by six bellies, / knowing which a twice-born reaches the supreme abode of Brahman:
"tat savitur vareṇiyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt".
Now the characteristic of the five-headed Gāyatrī: / "bhūḥ bhuvaḥ svaḥ mahaḥ janaḥ tapaḥ satyam / tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt".

One should perform the placement of syllables again with the Gāyatrī accompanied by the sacred utterances; / freed from all sin, he goes to union with Viṣṇu:

One should place: —bhūḥ on the feet, —bhuvaḥ on the knees, —svaḥ on the hips, —mahaḥ on the navel, / —janaḥ on the heart, —tapaḥ on the hands, —satyam on the forehead.
"tat savitur vareṇiyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt" / thus on the crest-lock.
The brāhmaṇa who does not know this is the lowest of brāhmaṇas; / his sin is not destroyed, [though] he may receive abundant gifts.
He who knows this Gāyatrī accompanied by all seed-syllables, / he knows the four Vedas, the knowledge of yoga, and the three muttering rites.
He who does not know this is regarded as lower than a Śūdra; / for that unpurified brāhmaṇa, ancestral offerings must not be given.
No one grants the fruit of bathing [to him], and everything becomes fruitless [for him], / since knowledge, wealth, and birth are the cause of twice-born status.
Everything is fruitless for him, like a pure flower on an impure thing. / In former times, the four Vedas and the Gāyatrī were weighed by me;

greater and weightier than the four Vedas, the Gāyatrī is remembered as the bestower of liberation. / With ten [recitations it destroys the sin] born of this birth, with a hundred that committed in a previous life,
and with a thousand, the Gāyatrī destroys the sin of three cosmic ages. / One who mutters the Gāyatrī on a rosary evening and morning
undoubtedly obtains the fruit of all four Vedas. / The twice-born who daily mutters the Gāyatrī at the three twilights for a year,
his sin arising from ten million births goes to destruction, / and by the mere utterance of the Gāyatrī he purifies [himself] from a heap of sins.
Muttering it daily, the best among twice-born attains heaven and liberation. / But one who mutters the mantras of Vāsudeva day after day,
and bows down at Hari's feet, would attain liberation. / If hymns to Vāsudeva and also his excellent narrative are on his tongue,
not even a particle of mud clings to his body. / By plunging into the Vedas and treatises, the fruit produced by bathing in the three-streamed river
is obtained by those reciting sacred duty in the world, [and] one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices. / Thus I am not able to tell all the virtues of a brāhmaṇa, O best of the twice-born!
He possesses the cosmic form; indeed, an embodied [brāhmaṇa] is Hari incarnate. / By whose curse there would be destruction of lifespan, knowledge, fame, and wealth,
and through his granting of boons all kinds of prosperity arrive; / Viṣṇu always attains devotion to brāhmaṇas through the grace of a brāhmaṇa.
Salutations to the deity benevolent to Brahmins, who works welfare for cows and Brahmins, / for the welfare of the world, to Kṛṣṇa, to Govinda, salutations again and again!
A person who constantly worships Hari with this mantra / is favored, and Hari takes him to union with Viṣṇu.
Whoever listens to this sacred narrative, the embodiment of dharma, / his sin that has been committed birth after birth goes to destruction.
He who recites it, or causes it to be recited, and is an instructor of people, / has no return [to rebirth]; he enjoys imperishable heaven.
He obtains wealth, grain, the enjoyments of kingship, and freedom from disease here, / a virtuous son, and auspicious renown, and he rejoices in heaven like a god.

1.47.m: Nārada said: / By your grace I have known the brāhmaṇa who is most holy. / That I may know, O Lord of gods, the lowest of brāhmaṇas by his deeds,
tell me quickly, O best of gods, if you have affection for me! / Brahmā said: / He who has abandoned the ten kinds of bathing, and likewise libations and other rites,
and who is devoid of twilight worship and self-restraint, is indeed the lowest of brāhmaṇas; / [and one who is] devoid of the worship of gods, vows, and likewise Vedic learning and other virtues.

And with truth, purification, and the rest, with practical yoga, knowledge, and libations to fire,
five baths for Brahmins have been proclaimed by the great sages:

The fiery, the watery, the sacred, the airy, and also the heavenly.
The fiery is the bath with ashes; the bath with water is called watery.

The sacred is indeed with [the mantra beginning] 'āpo hi ṣṭhā'; the airy is remembered as the dust raised by cows;
and the bath with waters from rain while the sun shines is called heavenly.

By bathing with these [methods] accompanied by mantras, one obtains the fruit of sacred places.
The water touching a tulasī leaf and the water of a śālagrāma stone,

the water from cows' horns, and water that has washed the feet of a Brahmin,
and likewise of paramount gurus, is traditionally taught to be purer than pure.

Whatever fruit a wise person attains through renunciation, pilgrimage sites, sacrifices, and the like,
as well as through observances, burnt offerings, and the like, that fruit [is attained] through these baths.

One who constantly neglects the offering of water to the ancestors
slays his ancestors and goes to hell; but one who lacks the twilight devotion slays a Brahmin.

Devoid of mantras and vows, and also of Vedic knowledge and virtues,
destitute of sacrifice, gift-giving, and the like, a Brahmin is the lowest of the low.

Those who sacrifice for wealth, temple priests, astrologers, village priests,
and those who constantly take pleasure in others' wives—these five are the lowest of Brahmins.

Devoid of Vedic mantras and purificatory rites, destitute of purity and self-restraint,
eaters of useless food, evil-minded, they are the lowest of Brahmins.

Foolish men intent even on theft, abandoned by all dharmas,
always walking on the wrong path, they are the lowest of Brahmins.

Destitute of rites like ancestral offerings, devoid of service to the guru,
without mantras, transgressing boundaries, all these are the lowest of the low.

These wicked ones are unfit to be spoken to; all of them go to hell.
They are impure, evil in conduct, and unworthy of worship on all sides.

Those who live by the sword, servants, twice-born men engaged in driving cows and draft animals,
those who subsist on artisans' labor, and those who are communal usurers,

those who traffic in children, those who practice sorcery, those who resort to outcastes,
those who are ungrateful, and those who slay their gurus—all these are traditionally considered the lowest.

And whatever others have ruined their conduct, are heretics and revilers of dharma,
and slanders of the different deities—these twice-born men are haters of the sacred.

Even so, a Brahmin must never be killed under any circumstances.
By killing him, O best of the twice-born, a person becomes a slayer of a Brahmin.

Whether fallen among the outcaste classes, among the barbarians, or likewise among the Caṇḍāla classes,
fallen through food or womb, he must not be killed under any circumstances.

Even after going to a woman of any caste, or eating anything inedible,
his status as a twice-born is not destroyed; through merit, he may become a Brahmin again."

Nārada said:
"Having committed such wicked deeds, if he afterwards practices merit,
what destination does that Brahmin attain, O grandfather of all the worlds?"

Brahmā said:
"Having committed all sins, he who afterwards controls his senses
is freed from all sins and becomes worthy of Brahminhood once more.

Listen, my son, to a delightful, wondrous, and ancient story:
There was a son of a certain Brahmin, endowed with the prime of youth.

Then, from the vigor of youth, delusion, and previous karma,
he at once went to a Caṇḍāla woman and became very dear to her.

He fathered sons and daughters with her;
having abandoned his own family, he lived in her house for a long time.

He did not eat the inedible food of others, and out of disgust he avoided liquor.
She constantly said to him: 'Drink some liquor or other.'

He then said to her: 'O dear one, you should not speak [to me about this] impurity.
Nausea constantly arises in me just from hearing of it.'

One day, exhausted from hunting game, he fell asleep in the house during the day.
Taking liquor, she laughed and poured it into his mouth.

Then a fire blazed forth from all sides out of the Brahmin's mouth;
and the flame burned her, along with her family, the house, and the property.

Crying out 'Alas, alas!' and rising up, the twice-born lamented then.
And at the end of his lamentation, he began to investigate:

'From where did this fire arise? How did the burning of my house occur?'
Then a voice in the sky said: 'This is the splendor of you, a Brahmin.'

When the event had been told as it had happened, the Brahmin fell into wonder.
Having reflected on the matter, the voice in the sky spoke these beneficial words again:

'Your great splendor has been utterly destroyed; therefore, become a practitioner of dharma.'
Thereupon the twice-born approached the best sages and asked about his own welfare.

All the sages said to him: 'Practice the dharma of giving.'
The ṛṣis said: 'Brahmins are purified of all sins through observances and vows.

Observe restrictions seen in the scriptures for the sake of purification:
the cāndrāyana and the kṛcchra penances, and the hot kṛcchra penances again and again,

and the prājāpatya penances, which are divine, for the swift drying up of faults.
Go to pure pilgrimage sites and perform the worship of Govinda.

Your sins will come to an end everywhere without delay,
by the power of holy pilgrimage sites and by the power of Govinda.

Your sins will come to an end, and you will attain Brahminhood.
Listen, dear one; we shall tell an ancient event as it happened.

Long ago, dear boy, Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā, sought food;
he was a bird, a fledgeling that had just emerged visibly out of the egg.

Afflicted by hunger, he said to his mother: 'Let food be given to me.'
Then, seeing Garuḍa, mountain-like and endowed with great strength,

the illustrious mother, joyful in mind, said to her son:
'I am unable to relieve your hunger entirely, my son.

Your father, righteous-minded, the grandfather of the worlds in visible form,
named Kaśyapa, practiced austerities on the northern bank of the Lauhitya.

Go there, ask your father according to your wish;
by his instruction, dear child, your hunger will subside.'

Then, hearing his mother's words, the son of Vinatā, of great strength,
swift as thought, went into the presence of his father in a moment.

Seeing his father, the best of sages, blazing like fire,
the bird bowed with his head and spoke these words to his father:

'I have arrived seeking food; I am the son of you, the great-souled one.
I am tormented by hunger, O protector; let food be given to me, O lord.'

Then, taking recourse to meditation and recognizing him as the son of Vinatā,
the best of sages, out of affection for his son, spoke these words:

'Many hundreds of thousands of Niṣādas, most sinful,
stand on the shore of the lord of rivers [the ocean]. Having devoured them, be happy.

Those irrepressible ones were destroying the sacred place, like crows of a sacred site.
Except for a Brahmin, eat them unnoticed among the Niṣādas.'

Thus spoken to, the bird departed and then devoured them.
A Brahmin who was unperceived was also swallowed by that bird.

That twice-born then stuck firmly in his throat;
and that best of birds could neither vomit nor swallow him.

Going to his father, he said: 'What is this, O father?
A creature is stuck in my throat; I am unable to remedy it.'

Hearing his words, Kaśyapa said to him:
'I told you before, dear child; this is a Brahmin, do you not realize?'
Having spoken thus, the wise and righteous sage said to the twice-born: / 'Come near me, I will bestow what is beneficial to you.'

The Brahmin then said to Kaśyapa, the foremost of sages:
'All these are my beloved relatives and constant friends—

fathers-in-law, brothers-in-law, trusted ones, and others along with their children.
Together with them, I shall depart either for hell or for an auspicious state.'
Hearing his words, Kaśyapa, astonished, said: / "Born into a family of twice-borns, you have fallen [to dwell] among Cāṇḍālas.
Those men are surely established in terrible hell. / There is no expiation whatsoever for them here for a long time.
Only when a man abandons all ill-behaved, evil-doing Cāṇḍālas / and evils, does he afterwards become happy, not otherwise.
If, out of ignorance or delusion, someone commits a dreadful sin, / and then practices dharma, he attains the highest state.
A sinner who does not practice dharma, but sets his mind again upon sin, / sinks in the ocean, just like one who has boarded a boat of stone.
Having committed all sins and an accumulation of wretched states, / if he afterwards becomes pacified, he will extinguish that fault."
The twice-born [Garuda] said to that very wise, best of excellent sages: / "If the bird here does not abandon me and all my kinsmen,
then I will give up my life, since the bird pierces my vitals; / otherwise, let him release my kinsmen; such is the vow of my firm mind."
Then, out of fear of killing a Brahmin, the sage said to Tārkṣya: / "Vomit them out everywhere, both the Brahmins and the Mlecchas!"
O lord of birds, in the forests, on the borders of mountains, and in the directions, / he, knowing what is wrong, quickly vomited them out by his father's command.
Then they all became manifest: hairless, devoid of beards; / and the Yavanas, delighting in eating, who had small beards;
and in the south-east [were] the naked sinners, and in the south the speechless, / dreadful ones, delighting in the slaughter of living beings, wicked-minded cow-eaters;
in the south-west [were] evil evil-speakers intent on slaying cows and Brahmins; / the fierce Kharparas dwell in the west and in the east;
in the north-west are the Turuṣkas, full of beards, cow-eaters, / mounted on horseback, who do not turn back in battle;
and in the north are mountain-dwellers, Mlecchas living in the hills, / eating everything, of bad conduct, devoted to killing and binding;
in the north-east are the Hells of tree-dwelling tormentors; / these terrible Mlecchas, with weapons in their hands, were placed in the directions,
by whose mere touch one must enter the water with one's clothes on. / And in the Kali age, in an untimely land devoid of dharma,
they even make contact everywhere out of greed for wealth. / But having released those Mlecchas, [Garuḍa], tormented by hunger,
the bird again said: "Father, hunger torments me exceedingly." / There Kaśyapa quickly said to Garuḍa with compassion:
"There are two vast creatures, an elephant and a tortoise, desiring to kill each other, / immeasurable, of great strength, in a certain region of the ocean.
Those two in the waters, dear child, will quickly ward off your hunger." / Hearing his father's words, he went there and seized the two.
Tearing the tortoise and elephant with his talons, that one of great strength and tremendous speed, / having held them, flew up into the sky with the speed of lightning, exceedingly powerful.
Mountains like Mandara and others could not provide a support [for him]. / Then, having traveled two hundred thousand yojanas with the speed of the wind,
the exceedingly strong one descended onto a huge branch of a jambu tree. / That branch suddenly broke; as it was falling, the lord of birds,
fearing the slaughter of cows and Brahmins, swiftly caught it, being powerful. / As he, exceedingly strong, was speeding rapidly through the sky holding that splendid [branch],
Viṣṇu, Hari having taken a human form, approached and said this: / "Who are you, and why do you wander in the sky, O lord of birds,
holding up a huge branch and the great elephant and tortoise?" / To him, to Hari bearing a human form, the bird replied:
"I am Garuḍa, O mighty-armed one, having the form of a bird by my own karma, / the son of the sage Kaśyapa, born from the womb of Vinatā.
Behold these two great creatures held by me for the sake of food; / neither the earth, nor trees, nor mountains can support me.
Seeing a jambu tree many yojanas high, / I descended upon its branch along with these two in order to eat them above.
That branch suddenly broke, and holding it I wander about. / From fear of killing tens of millions of Brahmins and cows,
dread and despondency suddenly entered me, O wise one. / What shall I do? How shall I go? Who will endure my velocity?"
When this was said, Hari then said this to the best of birds: / 'Mounting my arm, eat these two, the elephant and the tortoise.'
Garuḍa said: / "Oceans and the best of mountains cannot support me; / how then will you bear one of such great power?
Except for Nārāyaṇa, who else is capable of bearing me? / What man could stand in the three worlds who will endure my velocity?"
Hari said: / "A wise person should accomplish his task; perform your task now. / Having accomplished your task, O best of birds, you will surely know me."
Seeing him to be of great strength and reflecting in his mind, the bird, / saying "So be it," descended upon that mighty arm.
His arm did not waver at the landing of the lord of birds. / Standing there, he released that branch onto a mountain abode.
By the mere falling of the branch, the earth, along with its forests, mobile and immobile beings, / shook, and the oceans trembled.
Then he swiftly devoured both the creatures, the elephant and the tortoise; / yet he did not attain satisfaction, and his hunger was not appeased.
Knowing this, Govinda said to the lord of birds: / "Eat the flesh of my arm and be happy."
When this was said, abundant flesh of his arm was indeed / eaten by him out of hunger, O son, [yet] no wound remained on it.
The very wise one said to Hari, the guru of the mobile and immobile: / "Who are you, and what dear thing can I do for you now?"
Nārāyaṇa said: / "Know that I am indeed Nārāyaṇa, who have arrived for your benefit." / And he revealed his own form to him for the sake of conviction:
clad in yellow garments, dark as a raincloud, four-armed and enchanting, / bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, the lord of all the gods.
Seeing him, Garutmān bowed his head to Hari / [and said]: "What pleasing thing shall I do for you? Tell us, O Supreme Person!"
Hari, the lord of the gods of gods, possessing great splendor, said to him: / "Become my mount and friend, O hero, for all time."
The best of birds said to him: "I am blessed, O lord of the gods! / My birth is fruitful today, O Lord, having seen you, O master!
Having requested my parents, I will come into your presence." / Pleased, Viṣṇu spoke this: "Become ageless and immortal,
invulnerable to all beings; let your action and splendor be equal to mine, / let your movement be everywhere, and let all happiness be yours permanently.
May everything that is in your mind be quickly fulfilled! / You will obtain pleasing food according to your wish without hardship;
you will immediately free your mother from affliction, not otherwise." / Having spoken thus, Hari instantly vanished right there.
Tārkṣya too, having gone to his father, then related everything. / Hearing that, with a rejoiced heart, he spoke again to his son:
"Blessed am I, O best of birds, and blessed is your auspicious mother; / blessed is the womb and the family to which belongs such a son as you!"
He in whose family a Vaiṣṇava son, the best of men, is born, / having delivered ten million ancestors, goes to union with Viṣṇu.
He who always worships Viṣṇu, meditates upon Viṣṇu, and sings of him, / who always recites Viṣṇu’s mantra, and recites his hymn of praise,
who always partakes of his consecrated food, and fasts on the day of Hari, / is freed through the destruction of all sins; of this there is no doubt.
He in whose mind Govinda always abides— / he alone, the best of men, through merits attains servitude to him.
Having accumulated good deeds from thousands of ten million births, / and through the destruction of all sins, he attains the status of a servant of Viṣṇu.
Fortunate is that mortal in the world who attains likeness to Viṣṇu, / who is eternal, to be worshipped by the foremost of the gods, the lord of the worlds, Acyuta, the imperishable.
He with whom he is well pleased is the best of men indeed. / By many austerities, by dharmas, and by various sacrifices,
Viṣṇu is not attained by the gods, [yet] he has been attained by you. / Release your mother from the terrible affliction caused by her co-wife.
Then, having relieved your mother, you shall go to the lord of the gods.” / Having received his father’s command and having gained a great boon from Viṣṇu,
he went, delighted, to his mother's side, and bowing to her, stood before her. / Vinatā said: “My son, was your meal had today, and was your father seen?
Why was there a delay for you? I am indeed tormented with anxiety.” / Having heard his mother’s words, Garuḍa, smiling as it were,
recounted the account. Hearing it, she was astonished: / “How could such a difficult deed be accomplished by you in your youth?
Blessed am I, blessed is my lineage, that you became Viṣṇu’s friend! / Having received the boon, my mind rejoices seeing your noble self.
By your prowess, my child, both my lineages have been delivered.” / Suparṇa said: “Mother, what shall I do for you that is dear? Speak it at once!
Having done that deed, I will go to the side of Nārāyaṇa.” / Hearing this, the virtuous Vinatā said to Garuḍa:
“I have a great sorrow, my son; bring about a remedy for it! / She is my sister and my co-wife; by her a wager was formerly made against me.
I fell into her servitude; who will deliver me from this? / Having made the horse black by means of her sons, the great serpents, with their poisons,
she said at dawn: ‘This horse has become black.’ / Then I said there: ‘This [horse] is always white in brilliance.
Your word is false, mother.’ Then she made a vow. / Thereupon I made an oath to Kadrū, the mother of serpents:
‘If this horse of Hari becomes black, / then I will become your slave!’ So I said at that time.
Then, when that horse of Hari was made black by artifices / and by her deceitful sons, I entered into servitude.
At which time I give her the object she desires, / at that time I will be freed from servitude, O delight of the family!”
Garuḍa said: / “Ask her quickly, mother; I will provide the remedy. / I will devour those serpents; my vow is true!”
Then the virtuous Vinatā, afflicted, said this to Kadrū: / “Tell me your desired [object], O auspicious one, by which I may be freed from this distress!”
That evil-doing woman said: “Let the nectar be given!” / Hearing that speech, [Vinatā] became lustreless.
Then, approaching her son slowly, she said, grieving: / “The wicked woman asks for the nectar! My son, what will you do?”
Hearing her words, Garutmān, filled with great anger, [said]: / “I will bring the nectar; mother, do not lose heart!”
Having spoken thus, he went swiftly into the presence of his father: / “I will now bring the nectar for my mother’s sake, O sinless one.”
Hearing his speech, the sage said to the lord of birds: / “Far above the world of truth, fashioned by Viśvakarman,
is a delightful city, an assembly hall, for the benefit of the gods, / hard to reach with its rampart of fire, unassailable by Asuras and Suras.
