1.47.m:
For its defense, a mighty god was placed there by the gods; / whomever that hero looks upon turns straightway to ash.”

Suparṇa said: / “A boon has been obtained by me from Nārāyaṇa, O best of sages! / I have no fear here, dear father, even from the hosts of gods and Asuras.”
Having said this, Garutmān, drawing up water from the ocean, / entered the sky, and, swift as thought, the bird flew upward.
By the wind of his wings, much dust arose; / it did not leave his vicinity, but went towards him [in cloud].
Going there, the powerful one extinguished the fire with the water in his beak; / his eyes filled with dust, the god could not see him.
The powerful one struck down those guardian hosts and seized the nectar. / As the bird was carrying off the nectar, Śatakratu came,
mounted upon Airāvata, and spoke this speech: / ‘Who are you, taking the form of a bird, who forcibly carries off the nectar?
Having done what is displeasing to all the gods, how can you delight in living? / With my arrows resembling fire, I will send you to Yama’s abode!’
Hearing the words of Hari, the mighty one angrily said: / ‘I am carrying off your nectar; show your prowess!’
Hearing this, the mighty-armed one struck him with sharp arrows, / as a cloud [strikes] a peak of Mount Meru with a shower of water.
With talons resembling thunderbolts, Garuḍa tore the elephant, / and Mātali, the chariot, the wheel, and the gods marching in front.
That mighty-armed one, Mātali, and the bull of an elephant were stricken; / then all the hosts of gods were turned back by the wind of his wings.
Then Jiṣṇu, enraged, struck him with his thunderbolt; / yet the great bird was not shaken by the fall of the thunderbolt.
Seeing his thunderbolt futile, Hari then became afraid; / turning back from the battle, he vanished right there.
Coming with speed to the earth's surface to him who was proceeding easily, / that foremost of the gods said before all the hosts of gods:
Śakra said: “If you give the nectar now to the mother of the serpents, / all the snakes will surely be made immortal by her.
Your vow will be ruined, and your life will bear no fruit; / therefore, with your consent, O sinless one, I will take it back.”
Garutmān said: “At the moment when my virtuous, grieving mother is freed from slavery / before all the worlds, O Hari, you may take the nectar.”
Having spoken thus, the one of great valor went and then said to his mother: / “The nectar has been brought, mother; let it be given to her!”
Her heart blossoming with joy upon seeing her son with the nectar, / she summoned her, gave the nectar, and was then freed from slavery.
The grass, wood, creatures, beasts, and reptiles, / seeing [this], were all astonished, as were the gods and great sages then.
Having liberated his mother, Garuḍa attained great excellence; / in that interval, Śakra suddenly seized the nectar,
placing poison there, unobserved by her. / Kadrū, delighted at heart, eagerly called her sons,
and, joyous, placed the venom having the appearance of nectar in their mouths. / Their mother said to them: ‘O sons, let there always be in your race,
in your mouths, this divine presence, and let these drops remain pleased.’ / Then the great sages, gods, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and men [rejoiced]...
[The gods, siddhas and munis] said: 'Mother, let them be in our family by [your] favor.' / Dismissed by the serpents, the gods, along with the siddhas and sages,
went joyfully to their own abode; the serpents remained delighted. / But Garuḍa devoured the other snakes by force.
The rest fled into the directions, onto mountains and into forests, / into the oceans, into Pātāla, into holes, into hollows of trees,
and the remaining serpents settled safely in hidden groves. / Indeed, serpents were ordained as his food by the Creator for all time.
Having devoured the serpents and spoken to his parents, / and having honored the gods, he went to the imperishable Hari.
Whoever reads or even hears the auspicious deeds of Suparṇa, / freed from all sins, is honored in the world of the gods.
